subject: Biotechnology
title: DNA Forensics
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on DNA Forensics.

hook.text: A single hair left at a crime scene contains enough DNA to identify the person who left it.

buildup.text: DNA profiling compares short tandem repeats — regions where letter patterns repeat different numbers of times.

discovery.text: The chance of two unrelated people sharing a full DNA profile is less than one in a billion.

twist.text: The Innocence Project has freed over 375 wrongly convicted people using DNA evidence — justice corrected.

climax.text: Genetic genealogy caught the Golden State Killer in 2018 — using a public DNA database to find relatives.

punchline.text: DNA never lies — but how we use it raises big questions.

quiz.question: How did investigators identify the Golden State Killer?
options: They found his fingerprints at a crime scene
They matched crime scene DNA to relatives in a public genetic genealogy database
A witness identified him from a photograph

details.summary: DNA forensics uses unique genetic markers to identify individuals from biological evidence left at crime scenes. Short tandem repeat profiling analyzes specific variable DNA regions to generate a genetic fingerprint that can match suspects with extremely high statistical certainty.
details.whyItMatters: DNA evidence has revolutionized criminal justice by both convicting the guilty and exonerating the wrongly accused. Over 375 wrongful convictions have been overturned through DNA evidence in the United States alone.
takeaways: STR profiling analyzes variable DNA regions to create unique genetic fingerprints
DNA evidence can identify individuals with probabilities exceeding one in a billion
The Innocence Project has used DNA to exonerate over 375 wrongfully convicted people

faq.question: How does DNA profiling identify specific individuals?
faq.answer: STR profiling measures the number of tandem repeats at 20 or more specific locations in the genome. The combination of repeat numbers across all locations creates a profile so unique that the chance of two unrelated people matching is typically less than one in a billion.

faq.question: Can DNA evidence ever be wrong or misleading?
faq.answer: The science is robust, but human error in collection, processing, or interpretation can cause problems. Contamination, sample mixtures, and transfer DNA from innocent contact are challenges. Proper protocols and statistical rigor are essential for reliable results.
